objectives: Apply the three modes (conduction, convection, radiation).
Compute LMTD + UA for shell-and-tube design.

slides.title: Three modes of heat transfer
slides.body:
Heat moves through matter by three mechanisms:

• **Conduction** — through stationary matter via lattice vibrations / electron flow. Fourier's law: q = −k ∇T. Thermal conductivity k: metals ~10-400 W/m·K; ceramics ~1-30; insulators ~0.03; gases ~0.025.
• **Convection** — by bulk fluid motion. Newton's cooling law: q = h ΔT. Convective coefficient h depends on geometry, fluid, flow regime; **free** convection h ~ 5-25 W/m²·K, **forced** convection h ~ 25-25000, **boiling/condensation** h ~ 2000-100000.
• **Radiation** — by EM waves. Stefan-Boltzmann: q = ε σ T⁴ for blackbody. Important at high T (furnaces, fire) + in vacuum (solar collectors, satellites).

Most industrial equipment uses convection + conduction in combination. In a typical shell-and-tube exchanger, heat moves: hot-fluid bulk → hot-side film (convection) → tube wall (conduction) → cold-side film (convection) → cold-fluid bulk. The resistances add in series:

  1/(UA) = 1/(h_h A_h) + Δx_wall / (k_wall A_wall) + 1/(h_c A_c) + fouling resistances

**Overall heat transfer coefficient** U is the most-quoted heat-exchanger metric. Typical values:
• Water-water exchanger: U ~ 800-1500 W/m²·K
• Steam-water condenser: U ~ 2500-7500
• Air-water: U ~ 25-200
• Gas-gas: U ~ 5-50

U drives design + cost: lower U → larger area → bigger + costlier exchanger.

slides.title: Log-mean temperature difference (LMTD) + sizing
slides.body:
For a heat exchanger with hot stream cooling + cold stream heating, the local ΔT varies along the length. The right average for design is the **log-mean temperature difference**:

  Q̇ = U A ΔT_lm

with

  ΔT_lm = (ΔT_1 − ΔT_2) / ln(ΔT_1 / ΔT_2)

where ΔT_1 + ΔT_2 are the temperature differences at the two ends.

**Countercurrent flow** gives larger ΔT_lm than co-current for the same inlet/outlet temperatures → smaller required area → cheaper. Industrial preference is countercurrent.

**Multi-pass** (1 shell pass / 2 tube passes, etc.) is partly co-current + partly countercurrent. Apply a correction factor F (chart-based) to ΔT_lm: Q̇ = U A F ΔT_lm. F < 1; typical 0.85-0.95.

**ε-NTU method** (effectiveness-number-of-transfer-units) is the alternative when outlet temperatures are unknown. ε = Q̇ / Q̇_max relates to NTU = UA/(ṁ c_p)_min + ratio C_min/C_max. Charts give ε directly.

**Pinch analysis** (Linnhoff 1979) optimizes a whole network of exchangers by minimizing the 'pinch' between hot + cold composite curves. Industrial application: 20-40% reduction in utility consumption in retrofitted plants — major energy-efficiency gains.

slides.title: Heat exchanger types + selection
slides.body:
Common topologies:

• **Shell-and-tube (S+T)**: industrial workhorse. Tubes in a shell; one fluid through tubes, other through shell side. Multi-pass arrangements (1-2, 1-4, 2-4). Robust, high pressure, easy to clean (pull bundle). U typically 500-1500 W/m²·K for water-water; 100-500 W/m²·K for gases.
• **Plate-and-frame**: corrugated plates clamped together; gaskets between. Compact, high U (3000-7000 W/m²·K), easy to expand. Limited by pressure + temperature (~25 bar, 150 °C with gaskets).
• **Welded plate (no gaskets)**: higher T/P; harder to clean.
• **Spiral**: low fouling, good for slurries.
• **Air-cooled (fin-fan)**: large surface, free coolant, but low U; used for remote cooling.
• **Compact / printed-circuit**: micro-channel, very high area density, used in cryogenics + LNG.
• **Heat pipes**: passive isothermal devices; used in electronics + spacecraft.
• **Furnace**: radiative + convective; for cracking, steam reforming.

**Selection criteria**: ΔT range, fouling tendency, pressure, materials compatibility, footprint, capital cost, maintenance access. Tools: HTRI software (industry standard), Aspen EDR, Bell-Delaware method (shell-side rigorous).

**Heat-integration** at plant scale: pinch analysis identifies which streams to heat-exchange + minimum utility. Modern grassroots designs typically incorporate 70-90% of theoretical pinch savings; retrofits are constrained by existing layout.

question.question: Design a shell-and-tube heat exchanger to cool process oil
question.goal: Cool 25,000 kg/h of process oil from 120 °C to 60 °C using cooling water from 25 °C to 50 °C. c_p,oil = 2.0 kJ/kg·K, c_p,water = 4.18. Assume U = 350 W/m²·K. Use countercurrent flow.

steps.motivation: From hot-side: Q̇ = ṁ c_p ΔT.
Apply LMTD formula with the two ΔTs at the ends.
steps.reveal: ΔT₁ = 70 K (hot end); ΔT₂ = 35 K (cold end). ΔT_lm = (70−35)/ln(70/35) = 35/0.693 ≈ 50.5 K. (Closer to 50.5; ~51 K reasonable.)
A = 833,333 / (350 × 50.5) ≈ 47.1 m². A shell-and-tube unit of ~5 m² × shell area would need many tubes; e.g., 200 tubes × 19 mm OD × 4 m long = 47.7 m². Standard layout.

steps.prompt: If you switch to **co-current** (parallel) flow with the same inlet conditions, what changes?
steps.reveal: Co-current ΔT_lm = (95−10)/ln(95/10) ≈ 37.7 K. Required area = 833,333/(350 × 37.7) ≈ 63 m² — 34% larger than countercurrent. Why countercurrent is industry-default: same duty + same U + smaller area + lower capital cost. Plus countercurrent can achieve outlet temperatures crossover (cold outlet > hot outlet) which co-current can't physically.

question.question: A plate-and-frame heat exchanger has U ~5000 W/m²·K for water-water, vs ~1000 W/m²·K for a shell-and-tube of the same duty. Why prefer S+T anyway?
options: Plate-and-frame is limited by gasket materials in pressure (~25 bar) + temperature (~150 °C); fouling tendency higher in narrow channels; expensive material requirements (titanium plates for seawater) for chemicals service. S+T handles higher P/T, is more robust to fouling + dirty fluids, easier to clean (pull bundle), + has decades of design + maintenance familiarity. Plate-and-frame is preferred for clean low-P/T duties; S+T for everything else.
question.explanation:
Trade-off summary:

**Plate-and-frame advantages**:
- 3-5× higher U (corrugated plates + thin channels + induced turbulence)
- Compact: <30% the volume of equivalent S+T
- Expandable (add plates)
- Lower hold-up volume (good for hazardous fluids)

**Plate-and-frame limitations**:
- Gasket-limited P (≤25 bar) + T (≤150-180 °C with EPDM; ~250 °C welded)
- Narrow channels → high fouling tendency → frequent cleaning
- Plate materials must be compatible with both fluids (titanium for seawater = expensive)
- Pressure-drop higher for given flow

**S+T advantages**:
- High P/T: routine 100+ bar, 500+ °C
- Robust to fouling, dirty fluids, large particles
- Mature mechanical design + maintenance know-how
- Standardized (TEMA codes); easy spare parts

**Selection**:
- Clean, low-P/T, water-side: plate-and-frame
- High P/T, dirty, oils/gases, chemicals: S+T
- Cryogenic, very high area density: brazed-aluminum or printed-circuit
- Air-cooled: fin-fan (no water needed; remote sites)

Modern plant: mix of types optimized per service. Pinch analysis identifies *where* to exchange heat; equipment selection optimizes how.

Note: there's no 'best' type — selection depends on duty, fluids, site, economics.

slides.workedSolution: Plate-and-frame: high U (3-5×), compact, expandable; limited to ≤25 bar, ≤150 °C, low fouling tolerance. S+T: handles high P/T, dirty fluids, robust, mature codes (TEMA), standard maintenance. Selection per service: clean low-P/T → plate; high-P/T or fouling → S+T. Mix in industrial plants optimized for each duty.

question.question: Pinch analysis recommends a 'minimum approach temperature' (ΔT_min) of 10-20 K. Why not just 1 K to maximize energy recovery?
options: Lower ΔT_min → smaller driving force → much larger heat-exchanger area required (A ∝ 1/ΔT_lm). Capital cost rises faster than utility savings as ΔT_min → 0. The economic optimum (trade-off curve) is typically 10-20 K; some specialty applications (cryogenic, LNG, supercritical CO₂) use 1-5 K with compact / printed-circuit exchangers.
Heat transfer is not feasible below 10 K driving force.
question.explanation:
Pinch analysis (Linnhoff) optimizes heat-exchanger networks. ΔT_min sets the closest temperature approach between any hot + cold composite curves.

**Lower ΔT_min**:
- More heat recovery (less external utility)
- Smaller pinch separation → more sophisticated matches needed
- **Larger area required**: A ∝ 1/ΔT_lm. Halving ΔT_min approximately doubles A.

**Higher ΔT_min**:
- Less heat recovery (more external utility)
- Simpler network, smaller A

Capital vs utility cost trade-off: total annual cost = A × cost/m² + utility × $/kJ. Optimum occurs where d/dΔT (capital) = −d/dΔT (utility). For typical industrial cases:
- Refinery + petrochemical: ΔT_min ~ 10-25 K
- Pharma + fine chemicals: 15-30 K (smaller scale, lower utility cost)
- LNG / cryogenic: 1-5 K (extremely valuable cooling; compact exchangers economical)
- Distillation column reboilers/condensers: ΔT_min often 5-15 K

Low-ΔT_min designs require **compact heat exchangers** (plate-fin, printed-circuit, brazed-aluminum) with U up to 10,000-50,000 W/m²·K. Conventional S+T can't economically reach 1 K — area explodes.

New technologies (compact + additive-manufactured exchangers) are lowering ΔT_min targets in CO₂ capture, hydrogen, + heat-recovery applications. Economic ΔT_min is dropping over decades — a key efficiency-improvement frontier.

hints: How does area scale with ΔT_min?
slides.workedSolution: Lower ΔT_min → more heat recovery + less utility cost, BUT A ∝ 1/ΔT_lm → exchangers grow rapidly + capital cost rises faster than utility savings. Economic optimum balances both: typically 10-20 K for chemicals; 1-5 K only with compact exchangers in cryogenic / LNG / etc. Modern compact-exchanger technology is lowering economic ΔT_min in CO₂ capture + H₂.

question.question: Compute the log-mean temperature difference (LMTD) for a countercurrent heat exchanger with ΔT₁ = 60 K + ΔT₂ = 20 K.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain to a junior engineer why you should always run pinch analysis on a process before selecting individual heat exchangers. What goes wrong if you don't?
question.rubric: Mentions: pinch analysis (Linnhoff 1979) identifies the minimum theoretical utility consumption for a process by graphing composite hot + cold streams. Identifies the 'pinch' point where ΔT_min is achieved; above the pinch only heat exchange + heating; below the pinch only exchange + cooling. Common mistakes without pinch: (1) exchanging across the pinch wastes energy; (2) heating below pinch wastes external utility; (3) cooling above pinch wastes recoverable heat; (4) individual-exchanger optimization may miss network-level opportunities. Modern plants: pinch identifies the target (often 20-40% utility reduction vs ad-hoc design); HEN synthesis algorithms (Aspen Energy Analyzer, kbcAdvanced PINCH) generate candidate networks. Notes that pinch is for grassroots design; retrofitting is constrained by existing layout but still beneficial.
